content: The availability of contraceptive methods at the point of service delivery must be carefully considered. Recommendations are detailed in Section 7, categorized by contraceptive method type: intrauterine devices (IUDs), progestogen-only contraceptives (POCs), combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs), emergency contraception (EC), the Standard Days Method® (SDM), and male sterilization. Each subsection provides guidance on the timing of initiation, necessary examinations and tests prior to initiation, continuation, discontinuation, switching methods, management of side effects or dosing errors, and appropriate follow-up care. Additional remarks and foundational principles are included where relevant, along with comprehensive reference lists. The third edition of the Selected Practice Recommendations (SPR) incorporates evidence-based recommendations derived from a review of summarized epidemiological and clinical data, weighing benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, and the quality of evidence. Details of the development process for this updated guidance are available in the SPR Web annex. Examinations and tests prior to initiating contraceptive methods are classified as follows: Class A: Essential and mandatory for the safe and effective use of the contraceptive method in all circumstances. Class B: Substantially contributes to safety and effectiveness but may be implemented based on public health or service context. The risks of not performing the test must be balanced against the benefits of providing the contraceptive method. Class C: Does not significantly contribute to the safe and effective use of the contraceptive method. The examinations and tests outlined in Section 7 are intended for individuals presumed to be healthy. Those with known medical conditions or special circumstances may require additional evaluations to confirm their suitability for a specific contraceptive method. The Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) for contraceptive use, fifth edition (2015), provides further guidance on eligibility categories (1–4), which are frequently referenced in the SPR. These categories range from no restrictions (Category 1) to conditions representing unacceptable health risks (Category 4). For more information, refer to the MEC fifth edition. When applying the recommendations in this document to national programs, several programmatic considerations must be addressed, including informed choice, quality of care, essential screening procedures, provider training, and appropriate referral and follow-up systems. Practices essential for the safe use of contraceptive methods should be distinguished from general health-care practices unrelated to contraception. Good health-care practices should complement, not hinder, the provision of contraceptive methods. Introducing these guidelines into national programs requires a well-planned process of adaptation and implementation. WHO recommends a six-step process: advocacy planning, situation analysis, adaptation to local needs, implementation strategy design, pilot testing and evaluation, and advocacy and scale-up. This process should be collaborative and participatory to ensure ownership and buy-in from policymakers, professional bodies, and national experts. People with disabilities must have equal access to sexual and reproductive health care, including contraceptive services, as outlined in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD). Health-care professionals must not assume that individuals with disabilities are not sexually active. Contraceptive decisions should consider individual preferences, the nature of the disability, and the specifics of different contraceptive methods. For example, barrier methods may be challenging for those with limited manual dexterity, and combined oral contraceptives may not be suitable for women with impaired circulation or immobile extremities due to the risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Supported decision-making processes should be implemented when necessary, ensuring that decisions align with the individual’s will and preferences. Adolescents often face barriers to accessing contraceptive information and services, including restrictive laws, confidentiality concerns, and judgmental attitudes from health workers. Adolescents are eligible to use all contraceptive methods available to adults, and age alone should not be a reason to deny access. Programs must address the unique needs of adolescents, including their increased risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and their preference for methods that do not require daily adherence. Proper education and counseling are essential to help adolescents make informed and voluntary decisions. Efforts should also be made to ensure that cost does not limit access to contraceptive options. Expanding the range of contraceptive choices can improve satisfaction, acceptance, and prevalence of use. Social and behavioral factors, such as sporadic sexual activity and the need for discretion, should be considered when selecting methods for adolescents. Comprehensive education and counseling, both before and during method selection, are critical to meeting the specific needs of adolescents and ensuring informed decision-making.
